articles.title: A Portland building owner rented out a wall for advertisements, but the sign company surrendered its permit and left the wall unusable for ads for years; an Oregon appeals court upheld a $1,237,191.92 judgment
articles.summary: A Portland building owner has kept a $1,237,191.92 jury award against an outdoor advertising company after an appeals court found that the company acted
articles.body: A Portland building owner has kept a $1,237,191.92 jury award against an outdoor advertising company after an appeals court found that the company acted unfairly. The company gave up a state sign permit instead of returning it when its lease ended. In a ruling issued on November 12, 2026, the Oregon Court of Appeals upheld the trial court's decision in favour of building owner Jim A. Atwood, his trust, and J.A. Atwood Corporation against Lamar Obie Company, LLC. In an opinion written by Presiding Judge Darleen Ortega, the appeals court found that a jury could reasonably decide that Lamar had broken its duty to act fairly and honestly under the lease agreement. The company had removed the legal approval needed to display commercial advertisements on Atwood's property.The dispute involved a large brick wall on the west-facing side of Atwood's building on West Burnside Street in downtown Portland. The wall faced a parking lot at street level and could be seen by traffic heading east. According to Oregon Court of Appeals records, the wall had displayed commercial advertisements for decades. Rather than selling advertising space himself, Atwood rented the wall to advertising companies. These companies sold the space to advertisers and shared the money with him. In 2009, Atwood leased the wall to Onsite Advertising Services, LLC. According to an earlier 2025 Oregon Court of Appeals ruling in a related administrative case, In re Jim A. Atwood Trust, a system of cables, anchors, bolts, and lights was installed on the brick wall after 2009. This allowed printed vinyl advertisements to be stretched across the wall. Atwood paid back his tenant for the installation costs through lower rent.Highway designation triggers permit disputeThe legal problems began when West Burnside Street, also known as Highway 596, became part of the National Highway System and was designated a state highway. This change brought the wall sign under the Oregon Motorist Information Act. The law required the owner to obtain a state permit from the Oregon Department of Transportation (ODOT) by June 30, 2015. Because the wall was larger than the current size limits for highway signs, it could only continue displaying advertisements with a special state permit. This permit was available for older signs that did not meet current rules. In 2014, the lease was transferred to OnDisplay Advertising, LLC, which applied to ODOT for the permit.To complete the application, OnDisplay needed written permission from the property owner. According to the 2025 appeals court ruling written by Judge Powers, Atwood signed a consent letter stating that the "permit shall be in the name of: OnDisplay Advertising, J A Atwood, J A Atwood Corporation, their successors and assigns, as his or its interest may appear." A few days later, while the application was still being reviewed, Lamar Advertising bought OnDisplay's assets. These included the lease for the wall and the rights to the permit application. However, when ODOT issued the permit in 2015, it listed only OnDisplay as the owner. After OnDisplay informed the agency about the sale, ODOT changed the permit to list Lamar alone. It did not add Atwood's name or notify him about the change.Surrendered permit leaves brick wall unusableLamar continued to operate the advertising sign under the lease until 2019, when its business relationship with Atwood broke down. According to case summaries published by legal research platform CREdocket and Oregon appeals court records, Atwood told Lamar that he was ending the lease. He also asked the company to transfer the ODOT permit to him. Lamar refused to sell or transfer the permit. Instead, the company removed the vinyl advertisement, cables, and lights from the wall. It left only the anchors and bolts behind and asked ODOT for a relocation credit. Under Oregon law, a relocation credit allows a permit holder to remove a sign and move it to another location later. However, the existing sign must first be taken down.ODOT inspectors confirmed that the advertising equipment had been removed from the freshly painted brick wall. The agency then granted Lamar the relocation credit without informing Atwood. According to CREdocket's report on the November 12 ruling, Lamar could not even use the credit itself. However, giving up the permit permanently ended Atwood's ability to display commercial advertisements on his own building. Since the wall was larger than current state rules allowed, ODOT later rejected Atwood's application for a new permit. The Court of Appeals upheld that decision on administrative grounds in June 2025.Jury verdict survives nine appellate challengesAfter losing access to the state permit system, Atwood filed a civil lawsuit against Lamar. He argued that the company had broken its duty to act fairly and honestly under the lease agreement. Oregon law includes this duty in every contract. A jury agreed with Atwood and awarded him $1,237,191.92 in damages. The amount included compensation for advertising income he was expected to lose in the future. Lamar appealed the decision on nine separate grounds. The company argued that Atwood's expectations about the permit were not reasonable under the law. It also claimed that the award for future lost income was based on guesswork and that the trial judge had given the jury incorrect instructions.The Oregon Court of Appeals rejected every argument that was properly brought before it. Presiding Judge Ortega wrote that the jury could reasonably find that both sides had a shared and reasonable understanding of the agreement. Based on the 2014 consent letter and their business dealings, the parties could have expected that whichever company held the lease would not take away the permit the landlord needed to keep using the wall for advertising. The appeals panel also found that Atwood had provided enough evidence of future lost advertising income for the jury to consider it. The judges found no mistakes in the trial judge's instructions to the jury. Along with the civil lawsuit against Lamar, court records show that Atwood also filed a separate civil case against ODOT. That case involves constitutional and other legal claims related to the state's handling of the advertising permit.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Nvidia scandal just the tip of the iceberg? How China's spy machine plays a bigger game
articles.summary: In the world of espionage, the most dangerous spy is not always the one breaking into secret facilities or stealing classified files.
articles.body: In the world of espionage, the most dangerous spy is not always the one breaking into secret facilities or stealing classified files. Sometimes, it is the person who gets close enough to make powerful people let their guard down.If 'Dhurandhar' brought the world of undercover agents and intelligence games back into popular conversation, the allegations surrounding former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang could easily pass for a plot from a spy thriller. An extramarital affair, a Singapore-based chip company and suspected links to Chinese intelligence have turned a corporate controversy into a national security question, bringing Huang's three-decade reign at the world's most influential AI chipmaker to an end.But beyond the personal drama lies a bigger concern for Washington: How far might Beijing go to get its hands on America's most valuable technology secrets?From honey traps to cyberattacks, China's methods of spying have evolved over the years. The Nvidia controversy offers a look at how China's intelligence agencies operate and why American technology companies have become key targets. An old trick with a new targetHoney traps are hardly a new invention. During the Cold War, the Soviet KGB used attractive female agents, nicknamed 'ravens' and 'swallows', to compromise Western diplomats and officials. East Germany's Stasi had its so-called Romeo spies, who cultivated relationships with secretaries working in sensitive West German government offices. The objective was simple: obtain information through intimacy, trust or blackmail that conventional espionage might struggle to access.China has its own history with the tactic. One of the best-known American cases dates back to the 1990s. The FBI believed it had recruited a Chinese agent named Katrina Leung under an operation code-named 'Parlor Maid'. Instead, Leung seduced two of her FBI handlers and passed agency secrets to Beijing, according to David Wise's book Tiger Trap: America's Secret Spy War with China.The Nvidia controversy has brought this old playbook into the age of artificial intelligence. Former CIA station chief Keith Riggin, who later advised American businesses on Chinese intelligence threats, has warned executives about precisely this vulnerability. His advice to American businessmen travelling to China was blunt: "You don't get any better-looking when you go to a place like China."Riggin told Foreign Policy that he knew of at least 20 other executives who had fallen victim to similar operations. His former colleague Rudy Guerin, who led FBI China counterintelligence, said most executives they briefed did not take the threat seriously.That may be the oldest vulnerability in intelligence gathering. Firewalls can be strengthened, passwords changed and sensitive networks isolated. Human vanity, however, is considerably harder to patch.There is, however, an important distinction between an affair and an intelligence operation. It remains unclear whether Alice Huang was recruited before becoming close to Jensen Huang, whether Chinese intelligence discovered the relationship later and exploited it, or whether she independently approached the agency. The possibility that she was pursuing her own commercial interests alongside any alleged intelligence activity has also been raised. None of these explanations has been established publicly. Inside China's spy machinery: The MSS and its cyber armyTo understand why the Huang affair has caused such alarm, it helps to understand that China does not operate through one giant spy agency with a single switchboard connecting every intelligence operation. Its intelligence machinery involves civilian agencies, military intelligence organisations, cyber units and provincial-level operations, sometimes with overlapping responsibilities and competing interests.The most important civilian organisation is the Ministry of State Security, or MSS. Established in 1983, it is responsible for foreign intelligence, domestic intelligence, counterintelligence and counterespionage. Its work includes monitoring foreign governments, collecting political and economic information, identifying threats to the Chinese Communist Party and pursuing intelligence opportunities overseas.For years, the MSS was associated with a relatively cautious approach to intelligence gathering. Its methods were described as 'a thousand grains of sand', the idea being that countless small pieces of information could eventually produce a useful picture. Former US officials have told Foreign Policy that the agency became considerably more aggressive and willing to take risks, particularly after 2005, when it reportedly designated the United States as its principal adversary.But the MSS is only one part of the pictureChina's People's Liberation Army (PLA) has historically maintained separate military intelligence and cyber capabilities. Before its major organisational restructuring in 2015, the PLA's Second, Third and Fourth Departments had distinct responsibilities. The Second Department handled foreign intelligence and military reconnaissance. The Third Department, commonly known as 3PLA, was responsible for signals intelligence and communications monitoring, making it comparable in some respects to America's National Security Agency. The Fourth Department was associated with electronic warfare and computer network attacks.The former Third Department was particularly significant. A Wall Street Journal investigation by Paul Mozur and James Areddy described an organisation with operational units spread across China. Foreign experts estimated that it employed more than 100,000 hackers, linguists, analysts and intelligence officers across multiple bureaus and research facilities. Some facilities were reportedly positioned around Shanghai, including locations close to major communications infrastructure connecting China with the US.The system is not necessarily a perfectly coordinated machine. Australian security researcher Tobias Feakin, in his study Enter the Cyber Dragon, noted that China lacks a formal central mechanism equivalent to Australia's national intelligence assessment system for bringing information collected by different agencies together into one consolidated assessment. Provincial agencies also have their own networks, interests and capabilities.That leaves room for competition, miscommunication and even freelance intelligence entrepreneurs who may pursue their own commercial interests alongside state objectives. It also makes the task of understanding exactly who is responsible for a particular operation considerably harder. From hacking computers to entering boardroomsChina's interest in cyber espionage can be traced back to a military awakening during the 1990-91 Gulf War. Watching American forces use computers, precision weapons and real-time intelligence to defeat a largely Soviet-equipped Iraqi military made Chinese strategists recognise how technology could reshape warfare.The lesson was that a weaker power did not necessarily have to match America's conventional military superiority. It could exploit the vulnerabilities created by America's dependence on technology, communications and information systems.In 1999, two Chinese military colonels published Unrestricted Warfare, a book exploring how weaker powers could use unconventional methods to challenge stronger adversaries. Cyber capabilities, economic pressure and other asymmetric tools featured prominently in this thinking.The subsequent growth of Chinese cyber espionage demonstrated how those ideas could translate into practice.In 2013, the security firm Mandiant exposed a Chinese military-linked unit that had been hacking The New York Times. The newspaper had published an investigation into the wealth accumulated by relatives of then premier Wen Jiabao. Hackers were suspected of trying to identify the sources behind the reporting.The commercial world was not spared either. Networks belonging to mining companies BHP Billiton and Rio Tinto were reportedly penetrated by Chinese hackers during discussions surrounding a proposed merger. The episode raised concerns that commercially sensitive information could be exploited to influence a major business transaction."Foreign intelligence services have discovered that unclassified US government and private sector information, once unreachable or requiring years of expensive technological or human asset preparation to obtain, can now be accessed, inventoried, and stolen with comparative ease using computer network operations tools," a report titled Capability of the People’s Republic of China to Conduct Cyber Warfare and Computer Network Exploitation, had warned in 2009.“China’s development of its computer network operations capability extends beyond preparations for wartime operations. The PLA and state security organizations have begun employing this capability to mount a large scale computer network exploitation effort for intelligence gathering purposes against the US and many countries around the world, according to statements by US officials, accusations by targeted foreign governments, and a growing body of media reporting on these incidents,” the report added.Chinese intelligence gathering has not been limited to military secrets or government communications. It has also sought economic, technological and commercial information that could give Chinese businesses and the state an advantage. Washington's missing alarm bellsPerhaps the most troubling part of the affair is not what happened in Taipei, but what may have happened in Washington.According to Foreign Policy, US officials had been investigating Chinese dealings involving Nvidia for at least two years. The New York Times reported that President Donald Trump was personally briefed about Huang's vulnerability around a year ago. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also reportedly helped circulate an interagency warning this spring.Yet Huang continued to enjoy a close relationship with Trump and accompanied the president to Beijing for his May summit with Xi Jinping.Trump subsequently said he did not remember receiving the earlier warning. Why the threat may not be overThe first reason is that the investigation remains unfinished. The US Justice Department has not publicly established that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence operative. The extent of any damage, if there was any, is still unclear.The second is that Nvidia's problems extend beyond its founder. Huang's departure leaves a company that has become almost synonymous with the AI boom under interim leadership. Its November 17 earnings announcement will be closely watched as investors and regulators assess the implications of the leadership change.The third is that the alleged operation, if confirmed, would highlight a vulnerability shared by technology companies worldwide. AI, quantum computing, biotechnology and advanced semiconductor research are all potential targets for foreign intelligence services. Not every route into a sensitive company involves a sophisticated cyberattack. Sometimes it begins with a conversation, a business introduction or a personal relationship.The popcorn moment may be over, but the investigations are only beginning. Congress, the FBI, Nvidia's board and a growing number of lawyers will now try to establish what happened, what was known and whether anything was lost.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday reiterated New Delhi's tough diplomatic stance towards Islamabad as Punjab chief minister Bhagwant
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs on Friday reiterated New Delhi's tough diplomatic stance towards Islamabad as Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann sought the Centre's clearance to attend a conference in Pakistan.During the bi-weekly press briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that requests for political clearance undergo an assessment in line with India's broader foreign policy framework."When it comes to relations with foreign countries, we have a national policy and expect everybody to abide by it. As far as political clearances for dignitaries visiting abroad are concerned, an assessment is made by this ministry, in line with its overall policy and processed accordingly," Jaiswal said."As far as our position on Pakistan after the Pahalgam terror attack is concerned, it should be amply clear to all as to where we stand," he added.This comes after Mann said his office was preparing to formally seek clearance to attend the 4th International World Punjabi Conference in Lahore, Pakistan, scheduled from November 27 to 29.Earlier, Mann had confirmed in the Punjab Vidhan Sabha that he had received an invitation to serve as the chief guest at the three-day cultural conclave in Lahore."We will wait for what they say. Political clearance has to be taken," Mann said during a press conference, noting that his office was completing the necessary paperwork to submit to the MEA.While expressing his eagerness to attend, the chief minister had also called for the reopening of the Kartarpur Corridor, which remains suspended amid heightened India-Pakistan tensions, so that legislators could visit Sikh religious shrines across the border.Under Government of India rules (Cabinet Secretariat and MEA guidelines), all chief ministers, state ministers and state government officials must obtain prior political clearance from the Ministry of External Affairs before undertaking any official or private visit abroad, particularly to sensitive destinations such as Pakistan.Following the Pahalgam terror attack and the subsequent deterioration in India-Pakistan diplomatic and security relations, cross-border transit mechanisms, including the Kartarpur Sahib Corridor, were suspended by New Delhi.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, a security official reported on Friday.The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district, along the N-25 national highway. However, Dawn, quoting Balochistan police, reported that at least 16 people were injured, including three members of the border forces.The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing, identifying the suicide attacker as Osama Shahwani and saying he had joined the organisation in 2022.A security official, however, said Shahwani's name had appeared in a missing-persons case in 2024. The official alleged that the incident pointed to the BLA's recruitment of young Baloch men and its attempts to mislead authorities about their whereabouts.The injured were shifted to nearby hospitals for treatment. articles.title: Ex-Hamas bodyguard found guilty of knife attack in UK; faces extradition to Germany
articles.summary: A former bodyguard of slain Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, who was granted British citizenship in 2020, has been found guilty of attacking a bailiff with
articles.body: A former bodyguard of slain Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh, who was granted British citizenship in 2020, has been found guilty of attacking a bailiff with knives outside his home in Birmingham.He is also wanted in Germany over an alleged plot to assassinate Israeli and Jewish targets in Europe, according to reports by Sky News and BBC.Mohammed Alfatih, 40, was convicted by a majority verdict at Birmingham Crown Court of unlawful wounding, possessing two kitchen knives and criminal damage. He was acquitted of the more serious charge of wounding with intent.The incident took place on October 14, 2025, when bailiff Kevin Bucknall visited Alfatih's home over his wife's unpaid parking tickets. Court footage showed Alfatih holding a half-brick and two kitchen knives before smashing the window of the bailiff's van. Bucknall suffered a head injury and required hospital treatment, BBC reported.Alfatih claimed he acted in self-defence, telling the court that he wanted to scare the bailiff away after an altercation inside his home. He also cited traumatic experiences in Gaza and Egypt, including being shot and tortured.His defence lawyer, Kate O'Raghallaigh, argued that his past experiences had heightened his perception of danger and triggered fear and desperation.Former Hamas bodyguard faces extradition to GermanyAlfatih, also known as Mohammed Naim, was born in Germany but grew up in Gaza, where he worked as a bodyguard for Haniyeh, who led Hamas from 2006 to 2017. Haniyeh was assassinated in Iran in 2024.He is the son of senior Hamas official Basem Naim. Alfatih claimed asylum in the UK in 2014 and was granted British citizenship in 2020, Sky News reported.German authorities accuse him of playing a prominent role in an alleged plan to target Israeli and Jewish people in Germany and neighbouring Austria. He was arrested in London in November 2025 on a German arrest warrant.According to the German indictment, Hamas's military wing, the al Qassam Brigades, allegedly established weapons depots in Europe. The stockpile reportedly included a fully automatic rifle, 13 functioning pistols and more than 700 rounds of ammunition.Alfatih is accused of meeting an accomplice in Berlin twice in the summer of 2025, collecting five pistols and ammunition before transporting the weapons to Austria and storing them in Vienna.Sky News reported that German media had published images from a pre-recorded video allegedly recovered during the investigation. In the footage, a man identified as Alfatih is seen wearing a black balaclava and sunglasses and speaking Arabic while vowing revenge for what he described as the Israeli "genocide" in Gaza.The 40-year-old was also questioned by British counter-terrorism police over alleged Hamas-related material found on his mobile phone, including a video referencing the October 7, 2023, attacks and an image of an al Qassam Brigades fighter, according to Sky News.However, the UK police investigation into suspected support for Hamas was subsequently dropped.Alfatih is expected to be extradited to Germany after completing any custodial sentence imposed in the UK. His extradition proceedings have been put on hold pending the outcome of the British criminal case.The judge has adjourned sentencing until January 11 and remanded him in custody.A Home Office spokesperson said: "There can be no place in our society for those who engage in violence or seek to facilitate terrorist attacks against innocent people.""Hamas is a proscribed terrorist organisation, and we condemn those who choose to support its activities and further its aims," the spokesperson added.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New York lawyer opened a sealed attic in his new office and found a century-old photo studio; its rare Susan B. Anthony portrait sold for $35,990
articles.summary: New York attorney David J. Whitcomb uncovers a secret attic housing a vintage photo studio with historical artifacts, including a rare Susan B. Anthony portrait that sold for $35,990 at auction.
articles.body: A visit to a newly purchased office building led to an unexpected discovery for attorney David J. Whitcomb in Geneva, New York, in February 2021. While inspecting the third floor with a friend, he noticed a water-damaged drop ceiling that concealed a sealed attic. Inside, he found an abandoned photograph studio. Among the discoveries was a framed portrait of women’s rights activist Susan B. Anthony, taken by photographer James Ellery Hale in November 1905. According to One Source Auction, the photograph later became the collection's most expensive item, selling for $30,500 at auction on September 18, 2021.David Whitcomb discovered the hidden studio behind a water-damaged ceilingFox News reported that Whitcomb acquired the building in December 2020 to grow his business. NPR reported that neither the sellers nor the earlier owners knew the attic existed. It had been covered up by a ceiling while converting the third floor to an apartment. There were hundreds of photographs, frames, glass negatives, cameras, photographic chemicals, props, backdrops and studio equipment. There were some photographs that were intact and in their original frames. Documents inscribed with the name James Ellery Hale have helped in associating the items with his photography studio. According to Historic Geneva, he operated in the city between 1892 and 1920.The collection included a 1905 portrait of Susan B. Anthony Among the most important finds was a framed photograph of Susan B. Anthony. Hale took the picture of the women’s rights activist in November 1905 in Lochland in Geneva about four months before her death on March 13, 1906. According to the description given on the photograph collection page of the Library of Congress, Hale took the picture and the photograph is a gelatin silver print that captured Anthony reading a book. The Susan B. Anthony Memorial Association chose the picture as the original photograph of Anthony in 1907 and Hale copyrighted the picture the same year. A related manuscript found in the Library of Congress records, dated March 1907, explains why the organisation selected this photograph. The photograph was significant for the collection as it captured Anthony in her last days and the relation of Hale and the photograph to the women’s suffrage movement made the find even more historical.Susan B. Anthony’s framed portrait sold for $35,990 at auctionWhitcomb and auctioneer Aaron Kirvan of One Source Auction collaborated to locate and catalogue the collection. Finally, the auction house sold the discovery in 350 lots, which contained more than 1000 items. The framed Susan B. Anthony portrait fetched the top price of $35,990, inclusive of buyer's premium.The One Source listing shows a hammer price of $30,500 for the portrait, with a 17% buyer’s premium from the auction house and a 1% Invaluable convenience charge added on top of that price. Another copy of the official Susan B. Anthony's portrait was bid on by the buyers at a price of $7,670. There were also some other photographs and artifacts from the Hale studio on offer.The discovery preserved a forgotten part of Geneva’s photographic historyThe finding shed light on the work of James Ellery Hale and the relationship he had with the city of Geneva. Through the pictures, one could see the portrait photography and studio practices of the late 19th and early 20th centuries. There were also photos linked with the women’s suffrage movement and included those related to Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Elizabeth Smith Miller. For Whitcomb, a routine look around a building he had just bought turned into the recovery of a lost photography collection.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Friday played down the newly formed alliance between AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party leader Chandra Shekhar Azad ahead of upcoming UP polls.He also advised them to establish a sustained political presence in Uttar Pradesh rather than make appearances during election season."The election date will be announced before January 10. We are moving forward in collaboration with our previous alliance partners," Akhilesh said at a press conference."In fact, I would suggest that they establish a permanent presence here; it would foster better coordination and facilitate ongoing dialogue," he added.Akhilesh said SP and its INDIA bloc partners were already working at the booth level to take on the BJP."We, the samajwadis, will unite to take on the BJP, work to remove it from power, and ensure it is removed once and for all. The Samajwadi Party and the INDIA bloc are consistently working at the booth level, putting in dedicated effort. In politics, many visitors appear during election season. Some of these individuals ought to stay and work here. They should witness the injustice, atrocities, and persecution inflicted by the BJP government," he said.His remarks came a day after Owaisi and Azad announced the Samajik Parivartan Morcha, an alliance they said would provide an independent political platform to deprived, oppressed and marginalised communities.The two leaders also invited the SP, Congress and other parties to join hands to prevent the BJP from returning to power for a third consecutive term.Speaking to PTI Videos on Thursday, Azad said the alliance's fight was against the ruling party and not the opposition."I do not wish to fight against the opposition. The battle is against the ruling party. We have resolved to uproot the BJP. This alliance will drive the final nail into the BJP's coffin," he said.Azad also rejected allegations that his party was acting as the BJP's "B team" and questioned opposition parties over their decision to contest against one another in different states.He cited remarks by the Congress national president, who reportedly described the Aam Aadmi Party as the BJP's "B team" at a rally in Punjab.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Chuva causa alagamentos em SP e mais de 100 mil imóveis ficam sem luz na Grande SP; acompanhe
articles.summary: A Defesa Civil de São Paulo emitiu na manhã desta sexta-feira (13) um alerta de temporais para a região Sul e Leste da capital paulista, além da cidade de Diadema, na Grande SP.
articles.body:
A Defesa Civil de São Paulo emitiu na manhã desta sexta-feira (13) um alerta de temporais para a região Sul e Leste da capital paulista, além da cidade de Diadema, na Grande SP.

Chuvas de quinta-feira (12) deixaram 26 desalojados e um ferido no estado de SP ;

Na capital paulista, uma erosão na calçada da Travessa Cravo Bem Temperado, no Grajaú, Zona Sul da cidade, provocou a interdição de quatro residências;

Temporal de ontem provocou pontos de inundação e enchente e deixou veículos submersos em Mauá;

Um trecho da Rodovia Anchieta sentido Santos, na altura do Km 21, chegou a ficar alagado.

Mais de 100 mil imóveis estão sem energia elétrica na Grande SP após chuva

O número de imóveis sem energia elétrica na Grande São Paulo ultrapassou os 100 mil nesta sexta-feira (13), em meio às fortes chuvas que atingem a região.

Segundo o balanço mais recente da Enel, 103.968 imóveis estão sem luz na Grande São Paulo, sendo 89.993 somente na capital paulista .

Mais cedo, às 12h05, o Centro de Gerenciamento de Emergências Climáticas (CGE) colocou as zonas Sul, Sudeste e Leste da cidade, além da Marginal Pinheiros, em estado de atenção para alagamentos.

A chuva também provocou pontos de alagamento e congestionamentos, como na Avenida Professor Luiz Ignácio Anhaia Mello, em frente à estação Vila Prudente do Metrô, na Zona Leste.

Alagamento na Vila Prudente, na Zona Leste

articles.title: Residents say 250 trees were cut from an Ohio forest meant to buffer their homes from coal ash near drinking-water wells; a federal jury trial began November 9 over a lawsuit seeking $3.3 million
articles.summary: A dispute over the removal of around 250 trees from a forest near a former coal-fired power plant in Ohio has reached a federal court.
articles.body: A dispute over the removal of around 250 trees from a forest near a former coal-fired power plant in Ohio has reached a federal court. Residents of Pierce Township are seeking $3.3 million in damages from the property's new owner, alleging that it violated an agreement requiring the forest to remain largely undisturbed. The trial began on November 9 in Cincinnati, with a jury set to decide whether the company breached the agreement by cutting down trees and creating logging roads.According to WCPO 9's report, the forest is part of a greenbelt near the former William C. Beckjord coal plant along the Ohio River. Residents say the greenbelt was meant to act as a natural barrier between their community and the buried coal ash at the site. They are concerned that removing mature trees has damaged this protective area, which they wanted to preserve.The lawsuit was filed in 2019 by Neighbors Opposed to Pit Expansion (NOPE), a group of Pierce Township residents. The case names Commercial Liability Partners (CLP), a Missouri-based company that bought the 1,443-acre former power plant property from Duke Energy in February 2018. Although CLP owns the land, NOPE controls the easement governing the greenbelt.The disagreement centres on a 1986 agreement that required the greenbelt to remain in a "substantially undisturbed" condition. Residents argue that cutting down hundreds of trees and creating roads through the forest violated this condition. However, the company's lawyer has argued that the agreement does not specifically mention mature forests or trees.Residents say tree removal changed the forestAccording to the lawsuit, CLP removed roughly 250 trees from the greenbelt in 2019. The trees included walnut, maple, cherry and pine varieties. Some had grown to around 50 feet tall. The company also cut logging roads through the forest.Allen Freeman, chairman of the Pierce Township Board of Trustees, said the residents noticed the damage while walking through the property. He told WCPO that the company had started selling valuable materials from the land after taking ownership."In 2019 CLP had full title to the property, and they started basically on a process of selling anything that they could make money off of, and that included selling the hardwood trees," Freeman said, as quoted by WCPO9.He also described how the tree line had been cut down. "We were walking the site, and you could just literally see how the tree line was just shaved off. The backs of trees that were just cut straight down," he said.The residents say the damage was not limited to the loss of large trees. They are also expected to testify about the disappearance of tree cover, small flowers and vegetation on the forest floor. They have raised concerns about the loss of wildlife habitat, including areas used by wild turkeys, and the spread of invasive plants such as honeysuckle.The residents' lawyer, Dave Altman, said in his opening statement: "We wanted it to be left alone."CLP's lawyer Gregory DeGulis, however, said the wording of the 1986 agreement was central to the dispute. "Substantially undisturbed state is the main term we're arguing about," he said. He also pointed out that the agreement did not use the terms "mature forest" or "trees".Why the greenbelt matters to residentsThe agreement dates back to 1986, when Cincinnati Gas & Electric, the former owner of the power plant, began purchasing residential and farmland properties to expand its coal ash pits. The move prompted opposition from local residents and township officials, who threatened legal action.The two sides eventually reached an agreement that included preserving the greenbelt. Christopher Knoop, a former Pierce Township trustee and member of NOPE's steering committee, was the first witness in the trial. He said the residents' group was formed in 1985.Knoop told the court that the community had agreed to keep the property undisturbed because it was an important part of the township's character. He also described the forest before the tree removal as having a mature canopy, with seedlings and young trees growing beneath it. The forest floor was clean and did not have invasive plants, he said.Freeman said the trees and their roots were important to the area. He explained that the root systems helped hold the hillsides around the coal ash pits. The forest also provided a natural screen that blocked the view of the exposed ash areas.Coal ash ponds raise concerns about drinking waterThe dispute over the greenbelt is linked to wider concerns about the former power plant's environmental condition. Built in the 1950s, the Beckjord plant supplied electricity to hundreds of thousands of homes and businesses across southwest Ohio for decades. Duke Energy closed the facility in 2014.After its closure, more than five million tons of coal ash remained buried in artificial, unlined ponds along the Ohio River.Coal ash is the waste left behind when coal is burned to produce electricity. It can contain toxic heavy metals that pose risks to groundwater, soil and rivers. The ponds at the former Beckjord site are located beside the Ohio River, which supplies drinking water to more than five million people in Greater Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky.The ash ponds are also close to Clermont County's public drinking-water wells. Some are around 1,000 feet from the county's primary wells, which serve approximately 145,000 residents.Residents have raised concerns about the possibility of contamination reaching the water supply. In July 2020, people living nearby complained about clouds of coal fly ash blowing from the site. Fly ash is another by-product of burning coal and may contain contaminants such as mercury, cadmium and arsenic, as well as low levels of radioactivity.In February 2021, the plant's main smokestack fell into the Ohio River during demolition. The submerged debris took months to clear.Separate lawsuits seek action over coal ashThe current federal trial deals only with the greenbelt dispute. A separate part of the residents' case, which will be heard by another jury at a later date, concerns allegations that CLP failed to disclose information about digging up and moving coal ash around the property. Residents have also accused the company of using an underfunded corporate shell, New Richmond Development Corp., to limit its liability.Clermont County has filed a separate lawsuit against CLP, Duke Energy and another property owner. Filed on September 24, the case seeks to force the companies to clean up the coal ash before it contaminates the region's drinking-water supply.The county also wants stronger groundwater monitoring, updated emergency safety plans, regular preparedness exercises and a court-ordered plan to prevent contaminants from reaching public water supplies.The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency inspected the facility in May and found significant noncompliance involving two ash ponds. It issued a notice of violation in June.The greenbelt trial is expected to last a week. Meanwhile, residents say the dispute is about more than the trees already removed. They want the site to be managed in a way that prevents further environmental problems for the community.Freeman said the two lawsuits offered an opportunity to address problems left behind by the former power plant. He said the community needed to consider the effects of decisions made today on people living in the area 30, 40 or 50 years from now.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Piddington villagers vow ‘war isn’t over yet’ after Angela Rayner approves plans to house 1,256 male asylum seekers at former military site MoD Bicester; residents threaten legal challenge
articles.summary: Residents of Piddington have vowed to continue their fight against plans to accommodate 1,256 male asylum seekers at a former military site near their
articles.body: Residents of Piddington have vowed to continue their fight against plans to accommodate 1,256 male asylum seekers at a former military site near their village, insisting that their battle is far from over. The development received full planning permission from Communities Secretary Angela Rayner on Thursday, November 12, despite strong opposition from local residents.The decision concerns the former Ministry of Defence (MoD) site at Bicester in Oxfordshire, which is located close to Piddington. The village, home to around 350 people, had earlier staged a symbolic referendum in which residents voted to leave the UK in protest against the proposed asylum accommodation.While the planning approval marks a significant step towards the development, the Home Office has clarified that a final decision to proceed with the site has not yet been taken. Meanwhile, residents have indicated that they are preparing to challenge the decision through legal proceedings.‘This war isn't over yet’: Piddington residents react to planning approvalLocal opposition to the proposed accommodation has continued despite the planning decision. Residents have raised concerns about the potential impact on the small community, including public safety, infrastructure, traffic and environmental issues.Joe Marshall, a Piddington parish councillor, told BBC Newsnight that villagers had anticipated the approval despite their objections. He also questioned the planning process and alleged that the application contained several discrepancies.“The quality of the application is shocking, the discrepancies are all over the place. They've really not followed the right planning procedure. But regardless of that, we always knew it was going to be approved,” he said.Pointing to the conditions attached to the development, Marshall maintained that the residents' campaign was not over. “So, you know, this war isn't over yet,” he added.He also questioned whether the concerns of local residents were being adequately considered, arguing that the proposed development went beyond a typical ‘Not In My Backyard’ (NIMBY) objection.Marshall cited the potential increase in the local population, emissions from generators and the possibility of increased road collisions as some of the issues that had concerned residents.Piddington villagers threaten legal challenge against asylum accommodation plansThe planning decision has opened a six-week window during which it can be challenged in court. Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally has indicated that residents are considering further action and that ministers should expect a legal challenge.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, McNally said there would be “many actions” by villagers, although he did not disclose the community's immediate plans.He also referred to the Hillsborough Law, saying residents intended to invoke its principles as they considered their next steps.When asked whether ministers should be prepared for a legal challenge, McNally responded, “Absolutely, absolutely.”The proposed development has already faced legal scrutiny from campaigners. The group Wrong Plan Wrong Site has sought a judicial review over aspects of the Government's proposals, including concerns about the environmental assessment.Kemi Badenoch criticises Angela Rayner's decisionThe planning approval has also drawn criticism from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, who described the decision as a “betrayal of the women of Piddington”.Badenoch, who had previously visited the village, accused the Government of ignoring residents' concerns despite assurances that their objections would be heard.“When I visited Piddington I met a village terrified of what was about to land on their doorstep. The Government said it was listening, instead it's completely ignored this community's concerns,” she said in a social media post.She also described the decision as emblematic of what she called Labour's disregard for the law and the safety of women and girls.Why is the UK Government planning to house asylum seekers at former military sites?The proposed use of MoD Bicester is part of the Government's wider effort to reduce its reliance on hotels for asylum accommodation. Ministers are looking at former military establishments as alternative locations to provide temporary accommodation for people seeking asylum.Two such sites are already being used for this purpose: Wethersfield in Essex and Crowborough in East Sussex. The Government is also exploring the use of MoD Barnham in Suffolk and MoD Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire.The Home Office has said that the proposed Bicester facility would accommodate single adult male asylum seekers, aged between 18 and 65, if the site is taken forward. The accommodation is expected to operate on a phased basis, with security arrangements and facilities designed to minimise its impact on the surrounding community.A Home Office spokesperson said that the planning permission would allow the department to continue progressing the proposed use of MoD Bicester. However, the spokesperson clarified that a final decision to proceed with the site was yet to be taken.The department also said the Government was working towards a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, adding that more than £1 billion had been saved in costs since the election. This includes its commitment to closing all asylum hotels and moving towards alternative accommodation arrangements.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US agency urges owners of 7.2 lakh BMW cars to park vehicles away from buildings over fire risk
articles.summary: BMW has recalled 720,796 vehicles in the US due to a fire risk and urged owners to park their cars outside, away from buildings and other vehicles, until
articles.body: BMW has recalled 720,796 vehicles in the US due to a fire risk and urged owners to park their cars outside, away from buildings and other vehicles, until repairs are completed, Reuters reported.The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) issued the warning after identifying a potential electrical fault involving the vehicles' water pumps. The affected cars had previously been recalled in 2024 over a water pump issue but now require further repairs.According to the report, an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump could be exposed to water, potentially causing a short circuit and increasing the risk of fire, even when the vehicle is parked and switched off.BMW is still working on a fix for the latest recall and has reported 10 fire incidents that may be linked to the issue. These incidents occurred after the vehicles had already undergone repairs under the 2024 recall, the report said.NHTSA has advised owners of affected vehicles to keep them parked outdoors and away from buildings and other vehicles until the necessary repairs are carried out.Which BMW models are affected?The recall covers several models manufactured between 2012 and 2018, including:2012-2016 BMW 3 Series2012-2016 BMW 5 Series2012-2015 BMW X12012-2016 BMW Z42013-2017 BMW X32014-2016 BMW 2 Series Coupe2014-2016 BMW 3 Series Sportswagon2014-2016 BMW 328xi Gran Turismo2014-2016 BMW 4 Series Convertible and Coupe2015-2016 BMW 2 Series Convertible2015-2016 BMW 4 Series Gran Coupe2015-2018 BMW X42016-2018 BMW X5 xDrive40eYou use AI every day. articles.title: In 1949, 12-year-old Billy Gilbert hid a Mason jar in his Colorado home’s wall; a contractor found it 67 years later and returned his letter, penny and family photo
articles.summary: Discover the touching story of Billy Gilbert, a 79-year-old man who was reunited with a Mason jar containing his childhood treasures, including a letter, a penny, and a family photo, after 67 years thanks to a dedicated contractor.
articles.body: In 1949, a 12-year-old boy named Billy Gilbert folded up a typewritten letter and put it in a Mason jar along with a few small treasures. He then hid the jar in a basement wall of his family home in Pueblo, Colorado, where it remained for 67 years. According to ABC News, it was found by a contractor remodelling the house who tracked down Billy and gave it back. By then, Billy was 79 years old.A letter from a 12-year-old boy The letter begins with simple facts. Billy wrote that the house was built in 1929 and that his family name was Gilbert. He also mentioned that they were four in total, including his sister Janice, who was 14 at the time. He added the year as 1949 and wrote about his pets, which included an Irish setter, two cats, and a bird. He even talked about how he had a stamp collection. The letter didn't talk about anything fancy; it was just about a young boy explaining who he was and what filled his days. Besides the letter, the jar also had a few keepsakes: an 1892 stamp from the stamp collection, an Indian Head penny, and a black-and-white picture of his family. By 1949, the stamp was already 57 years old. The Indian Head pennies were made between 1859 and 1909, making the coin at least 40 years old. Sadly, his sister has since died, and Billy was the only family member left from that photo.The contractor who went looking The contractor who was remodelling the home, Mark Knecht, found the jar and knew immediately he had to find its owner. He found Billy online, which he said took only about 10 minutes. Billy, however, saw things differently. In his view, Mark could have thrown away the jar, but instead he spent a lot of time and effort finding him. Billy was living in Sammamish, Washington, at the time. Distance was no obstacle. Mark was already planning a trip to the Seattle area with his daughter. Billy said he would pay for the jar to be posted, but Mark insisted he would bring it over himself. NBC News, in a report by KING’s Ted Land, described the jar as a homemade capsule, and both networks covered the story on January 19, 2016.A day Billy called amazing For Billy, the delivery was a flood of memories. He admitted to ABC News, “I hadn't even remembered writing the letter.” Still, looking at the souvenirs brought back a lot of memories. He described it as an amazing day and spoke warmly of Mark. The find was just as important for Mark. He said it was the coolest thing he had ever found, adding that he had torn apart plenty of houses without ever coming across anything like it. It's not hard to see why. The jar contained a boy’s own words, and this time there was someone to carry them back to him. In today's world of cloud storage and phone galleries, Billy’s jar held life as it was for him back in 1949. He got a letter back, a stamp, a penny, a photo of his family and a whole lot of memories. Those details are small, but they connect a boy, a house, and a stranger who cared enough to make the journey.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2022, Kansas backed a $160 million lagoon resort and sold $35.3 million in bonds; four years later, with no buildings on the site, the state is suing to block further public spending
articles.summary: State officials in Kansas have filed a lawsuit to stop more public bond money from going to Derby Shores, a planned $160 million lagoon resort.
articles.body: State officials in Kansas have filed a lawsuit to stop more public bond money from going to Derby Shores, a planned $160 million lagoon resort. The project still has no buildings above ground, four years after it was approved. The Kansas Department of Commerce filed the lawsuit this month in Sedgwick County District Court. It is asking the court to block any more bond payments and require a full account of the $35,285,000 in bonds already sold for the project. "More than four years after the project was approved and bonds were sold, it has not been built," the state said in its court filing. "Announced opening dates have come and gone."The lawsuit names Derby Destination Development, a partnership made up of Dave Murfin, Rick Worner, and Rodney Steven II. Project trustee Security Bank of Kansas City and the city of Derby are also named as defendants, according to The Wichita Eagle. Derby city manager Kiel Mangus said local officials are still reviewing the lawsuit and waiting for the private developers to take action. "It is going to take action by the developer to move things forward," Mangus told The Wichita Eagle. "We haven’t fully been able to evaluate all the things in the suit, so that’s what we’re going through right now," he added. He also said: "We’re hopeful that we can find a resolution and move forward in an acceptable manner to all parties." None of the developers, a Department of Commerce spokesperson, or the agency's two lawyers from Morris Laing returned calls for comment on Wednesday, The Wichita Eagle reported.Grand resort plans and rising costsDerby Shores was first presented as a major tourist attraction for the region. Its main feature would be a 4 1/2-acre lagoon with water activities. The plans also include a hotel, apartments, housing for older people, restaurants along the water, a tiki bar, a climbing wall, a zipline, an aerial ropes park, a BMX course, a camping area, a picnic lawn, and an outdoor space for events. The entire development would cover about 40 acres. The original project budget was $130 million. Murfin and Worner later brought in Steven, the founder of the Genesis Health Clubs chain, which has nearly 90 locations across the country, to develop one part of the project. Steven took charge of building and operating the lagoon and increased its planned size from 2 acres.Steven also operates the Genesis Sports Complex and Blast Off Bay water park in Goddard. Speaking to The Wichita Eagle in 2024, he explained why he wanted a larger lagoon. "I didn’t think it would be enough of a draw," Steven said. "I just wanted to do it right. I didn’t want to do something little." The resort is part of a larger $100 million sales tax and revenue (STAR) bond district created by Derby in 2018. The district was originally established to support Worner's Field Station: Dinosaurs attraction. That dinosaur park has already paid off its bond debt. However, The Wichita Eagle reported that it now faces possible closure because of financial problems that began during the pandemic.Dispute over construction deadlines and taxpayer riskUnder Kansas's STAR bond programme, future sales tax money collected inside a special district is used to repay project bonds instead of going into the State General Fund. State lawmakers require construction to begin within two years after a project plan is approved because public tax money is used to support the debt. "Kansas taxpayers carry most of that cost," the Department of Commerce argued in its lawsuit. "The sales tax that repays STAR bonds would otherwise go to the State General Fund. Because the State takes that risk, the Legislature attached conditions to STAR bond projects." The lawsuit also quotes the law, which states that if construction does not begin within two years, "funding for such project shall cease." According to the lawsuit, Derby approved the project plan on May 10, 2022. A total of $35,285,000.00 in bonds were sold in July 2022. Lawyers representing the developers argued that construction began in January 2023, when workers demolished a barn and farmhouse on the property. State officials disagreed with this claim. They pointed out that "The City’s own 2026 report to the State says construction began in 2026."Site conditions and scope of the state injunctionMangus said that infrastructure work, including roads, drainage systems, land grading, and sewers, is "nearly complete." However, the lawsuit states that no buildings have been constructed above ground and that "ground cleared in the past has gone back to weeds." Although the state wants a temporary and possibly permanent stop to further bond payments, officials said they are not trying to shut down the wider development district or prevent work paid for with private money. According to the court filing, "Commerce is not seeking to end the Derby STAR Bond District, cancel Derby’s agreements, or stop the developer or anyone else from building with private funds."The department is also not asking for the return of bond money that has already been properly spent on approved project costs. It is not trying to stop the developer from applying for fresh project approval under the STAR Bond Act either. Instead, the lawsuit states that if the legal requirements are not met, "Commerce asks that the unexpended proceeds be applied to retiring the bonds that were issued to fund it." Derby has asked the state to remove its order stopping further bond payments. The developers have also urged the city to restart the payments. The state warned that "and the public will suffer irreparable injury" if spending continues without proper checks. In its filing, the department defended its request, stating: "The injunction serves the public interest. It enforces the Act as the Legislature wrote it. It preserves public funds that are repaid primarily with state sales tax revenue. . . . It preserves, rather than forecloses, the ability of the Secretary to approve the project again if the Act’s requirements are met."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: ‘Operate solely in English’: Trump admin asks US agencies to ditch foreign-language materials; over 27 million could be affected
articles.summary: The Trump administration has directed US federal agencies to prioritise English in government operations and restrict the use of foreign-language
articles.body: The Trump administration has directed US federal agencies to prioritise English in government operations and restrict the use of foreign-language materials, in a move that could affect more than 27 million people with limited English proficiency in the country.“Agencies should strive to operate solely in English,” the Justice Department said in fresh guidance issued on Thursday, according to a New York Post report. The directive asks agencies to provide a wide range of government materials exclusively in English, including official correspondence, regulations, public announcements, applications, websites, educational resources and internal communications.The guidance also extends to artificial intelligence tools used by federal agencies, marking a broader push to make English the default language across government operations.The latest directive seeks to implement President Donald Trump's March 2025 executive order that designated English as the official language of the US. The order reversed a decades-old federal policy aimed at improving access to government services for people who have limited English proficiency.While Trump's original executive order did not require agencies to discontinue existing multilingual services, the new Justice Department guidance encourages them to operate primarily in English. It says agencies should provide services in other languages only when required by law or necessary to fulfil their missions, including in areas such as national security and healthcare.More than 27 million people could be affectedThe changes could have implications for more than 27 million people in the US who have limited ability to speak, read or write English.Some federal agencies have already begun removing non-English resources. The General Services Administration (GSA), earlier this week, shut down the Spanish-language version of USA.gov, the government's official information portal, and began redirecting visitors to its English-language version. The Spanish website was first launched in 2003.The Department of Housing and Urban Development had also moved over the summer to remove non-English languages from its services, according to the report.Jacob Hofstetter, a policy analyst specialising in language access at the Migration Policy Institute, warned that the latest guidance could accelerate the removal of multilingual government resources.“I would be surprised if we didn’t see more agencies taking down multilingual content or trying to reduce the level of language access they provide,” he said.The Justice Department has invited public comments on the memorandum until January 11. However, a department spokesperson told The Washington Sun that the guidance was final and already in effect. The memorandum was issued to federal agencies in September and made publicly available on Thursday.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Georgia towns opposed plans to turn two huge warehouses into ICE detention centers, including one designed for up to 10,000 people; the federal government has now listed both properties for sale
articles.summary: Federal officials have officially cancelled plans to turn two large warehouses in Georgia into immigration detention centres.
articles.body: Federal officials have officially cancelled plans to turn two large warehouses in Georgia into immigration detention centres. Both properties have now been listed for sale following strong public and political opposition. The decision is a major win for local communities in Douglas and Jackson counties, which strongly opposed the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposal. The cancelled plan included turning a huge warehouse in Lithia Springs into a detention centre that could hold up to 10,000 people. Critics described it as a "mass incarceration" facility that would change the character of the community. The U.S. General Services Administration (GSA), the federal agency that manages government property, confirmed that both the Lithia Springs warehouse and another large property in Braselton are now considered surplus government property and are available for sale.The massive detention center projectThe federal plan first emerged in 2020 and 2021. It was part of a wider ICE effort to change how immigration detention was handled. According to reports from the American Immigration Council, the agency wanted to move towards government-owned, modular processing centres. These centres would be created by changing commercial warehouses to meet detention needs. ICE wanted facilities that could easily expand or adjust to changing operational needs. The planned facilities were much larger than anything previously proposed in the region. CBS News Atlanta previously reported that the Lithia Springs warehouse in Douglas County was bought in 2020 for nearly $13.5 million. Its design included modular sections that could allow it to hold up to 10,000 people. The building covered more than 360,000 square feet and was expected to become a leading example of this new approach to immigration enforcement away from the border. Federal officials also bought a second warehouse in Braselton, Jackson County. The property covered more than 500,000 square feet and cost $11 million in 2021. Both purchases were made quietly, often surprising local leaders. MPB News reported earlier this year that similar buying methods had been used in several other towns targeted for detention centre expansion.Fierce opposition by local communitiesResidents and elected officials across Georgia joined together to oppose the federal plans from the beginning. In Douglas County, commissioners and local residents raised serious concerns about public safety, property values, and the impact of having such a large detention centre in their community. Douglas County Commissioner Kelly Mitchell-Garnett summed up the community's position when speaking to federal officials. "We simply don’t want it," she said. The county commission passed resolutions against the project. Officials argued that the warehouse was too close to homes and schools. Congressman David Scott also played an important role by working in Congress to stop the conversion plans or prevent public money from being used for them, CBS News Atlanta reported. Residents in Braselton also strongly opposed the proposal. Jackson County residents filled local public meetings to speak against having a federal detention centre in their town. They argued that such a facility would change the peaceful nature of their community and put extra pressure on local infrastructure and services.Government waste expose and plan scrappedThe decision to sell the properties comes after years of delays and growing concerns about wasted government money. Last month, the GSA officially listed both properties for sale. This happened after federal officials informed leaders in Oakwood and Social Circle, two other locations previously considered for detention centres, that the warehouse purchase programme was being brought to an end. Concerns about poor financial management also played an important part in the cancellation. CBS News Atlanta previously reported that the federal government was spending millions of taxpayer dollars to maintain warehouses that were sitting empty. A Government Accountability Office report released in September confirmed that federal agencies had lost $20 million in costs that could not be recovered after purchasing warehouses they no longer planned to use. Rep. Scott welcomed the decision, saying he had long argued that the Douglas County property was not suitable for a detention centre. He was pleased that ICE would not move ahead with the Lithia Springs project. Speaking to CBS News Atlanta, he said: "The plan to open an ICE processing facility in Douglas County is dead. I am proud to have led the fight to block this facility that didn’t belong in our district, and I’m glad our community won’t have to live under that threat anymore." Douglas County commissioners also welcomed the announcement that the property would be sold. Commissioner Tarenia Carthan shared her relief and happiness in a Facebook post. She described the warehouse receiving official surplus status and being listed for sale as a final victory for the community.Future use of massive warehouse sitesThe GSA is now working to sell the properties as quickly as possible. The Braselton warehouse includes light industrial space and offices, according to federal records. It is being sold through a public auction, with a starting bid of $11 million listed by FOX 5 Atlanta. articles.title: A routine pipeline excavation near a German swimming pool led to the discovery of 1,600 medieval silver coins that could have bought 150 sheep
articles.summary: A construction worker discovered approximately 1,600 medieval coins while overseeing pipeline installation near a swimming pool in Glottertal, Germany.
articles.body: A construction worker discovered approximately 1,600 medieval coins while overseeing pipeline installation near a swimming pool in Glottertal, Germany. The find, dating to around 1320, included coins from several regional mints and is considered one of the most extensive medieval coin hoards discovered in the region in recent decades. According to the Stuttgart Regional Council, the discovery began when Glottertal resident Claus Völker spotted small metal objects in excavated material in May 2024. Archaeologists and certified metal detectorists subsequently recovered around 1,000 coins, followed by another 600. An archaeologist said the collection could have bought approximately 150 sheep at the time.Archaeologists recovered around 1,000 silver coinsThe discovery was made by Glottertal resident Claus Völker, who accompanied pipeline installation work near the local swimming pool in early May 2024. He was present at the request of an employee of the State Office for the Preservation of Historical Monuments (LAD).While observing the excavated material, Völker noticed what appeared to be small metal plates. He subsequently inspected the pipeline trench, where he discovered additional objects, and immediately reported the findings to the LAD.Representatives from the authority visited the location on the same day and recovered approximately 1,000 coins. The discovery prompted further archaeological investigations to establish whether additional coins remained in the excavated soil.Metal detectorists recovered 600 additional coinsFollowing the initial discovery, three metal detectorists certified by the State Office for the Preservation of Historical Monuments were commissioned to examine the excavated material.The search continued despite difficult conditions, with rain turning the spoil heap into knee-deep mud. Nevertheless, the investigators continued their work and recovered approximately 600 additional coins.The combined discoveries brought the total to around 1,600 coins, making the find one of the most extensive medieval coin hoards discovered in the region in recent decades.The Stuttgart Regional Council credited Völker's careful observation and the subsequent archaeological investigation for the discovery and recovery of the collection.Archaeologists traced the silver coins to several medieval European citiesFollowing preliminary cleaning, archaeologists were able to identify the origins of most of the coins. Andreas Haasis-Berner, an archaeologist at the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology (LAD), said the collection predominantly contained coins from the mints of Breisach, Zofingen and Freiburg.These coins were minted around 1320. The collection also included smaller numbers of coins from Basel, St. Gallen, Zurich, Laufenburg and Colmar.The different minting locations provide archaeological material for examining the circulation of coins across the Breisgau region during the medieval period.1,600 coins could have purchased approximately 150 sheep in medieval timesExplaining the significance of the discovery, Haasis-Berner said the analysis of the hoard could provide insights into several aspects of the region's medieval economy.According to the archaeologist, studying the collection would help researchers understand coin circulation in the Breisgau region, minting activities at different mints, the silver trade and mining in the Glotter Valley.The discovery also offers information about the purchasing power of silver coins during the period. When asked about the hoard's value at the time, Haasis-Berner explained that the coins could have bought approximately 150 sheep.The archaeological examination of the collection is therefore expected to contribute to the understanding of medieval economic activity and monetary circulation in southwestern Germany.The Stuttgart Regional Council published photographs of the recovered coins alongside its August 12, 2024, announcement, including examples identified as Breisach and Zofingen types.You use AI every day. articles.title: A 92-year-old Florida woman was still working at a clothing store because she could not afford to retire; a stranger's fundraiser raised $120,000, and neighbours helped repair her home
articles.summary: Muriel Connick, a 92-year-old Florida woman, continued working at a clothing store because she could not afford to retire, even as the demands of the job
articles.body: Muriel Connick, a 92-year-old Florida woman, continued working at a clothing store because she could not afford to retire, even as the demands of the job became increasingly difficult. Her circumstances changed after a chance encounter with April Steele, a shopper who learnt about Connick’s financial struggles and decided to help. What began as a small fundraising effort grew into a campaign attracting more than $120,000 in donations. The support did not stop at helping Connick leave work, with neighbours and local businesses also coming together to repair her deteriorating home.How a 92-year-old Florida woman found help to retireConnick was working at a Burlington clothing store in Pompano Beach when she met Steele, who was shopping at the store. According to GoFundMe, she noticed the elderly employee working in the fitting rooms and initially tried to compliment her on still being employed at her age.The conversation took an unexpected turn when Connick responded that she did not want to work at 92 but had no choice. Steele learnt that Connick’s pension and food assistance had been reduced, leaving her struggling to make ends meet.The encounter left Steele concerned about the older woman’s circumstances. She later returned to the store with a small gift after posting about Connick’s situation on Facebook. The response encouraged her to do more, eventually leading her to create a fundraiser.Steele explained on the GoFundMe campaign that she was not related to Connick and had simply met her while shopping. Her initial appeal was modest, intended to raise a few thousand dollars to help the woman enjoy retirement.A small fundraiser attracted thousands of donorsThe campaign quickly gained attention as Connick’s story reached people beyond Pompano Beach. The GoFundMe page, titled Help Muriel Ann Connick, a 92 year old lady retire, described her financial difficulties and the physical demands of continuing to work at such an advanced age.Steele highlighted the challenge of spending long hours on her feet, pointing out that even someone considerably younger would find the work tiring. She appealed to people who could afford to contribute to help Connick spend her remaining years without having to continue working.The fundraiser eventually exceeded its original $10,000 target by a considerable margin. WSVN reported on March 11 that donations had passed $120,000.Why did Connick's home need repairsThe financial assistance was not the only challenge Connick faced. Her mobile home also required significant repairs, with damaged flooring linked to broken pipes underneath the property.A message from one of Connick’s former co-workers on GoFundMe explained that the plumbing problem was causing the floors to deteriorate, creating a serious risk of falls. The co-worker said Connick had sought assistance through Burlington’s support fund but had been denied help.The same message noted that she needed around $5,000 to repair the pipes and was trying to gather a $2,000 down payment for a contractor. The condition of the home added another layer of difficulty to her situation, particularly given her age and limited finances.Neighbours and businesses joined the home renovationBy March, the campaign had developed into a broader effort to improve Connick’s living conditions. WSVN reported that construction crews had begun working on her mobile home, with several local businesses contributing labour and materials.The renovation involved removing damaged flooring down to the subfloor, laying new plywood and installing replacement floors. Bob Stenbeck of Bobkat Construction and Adam Morgenstern of Elevated Construction were among those helping with the project.Stenbeck said his company wanted to give something back to the community after hearing about Connick’s circumstances. He felt that someone should not have to work until the age of 92 simply to meet basic expenses.Other companies involved included New Creations Design and Construction, LW Flooring, Rocksteady Consulting, Padilha Construction and Heartland Flooring Solutions.According to WSVN, she stopped working a few weeks before the March report and was officially retired. She thanked everyone who had contributed. Steele admitted she had never expected her initial effort to grow into something so significant.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
